strengths: The core idea—discarding the encoder and directly optimizing manifold-valued latents via Riemannian optimization (building on the Deep Generative Decoder)—is simple, elegant, and immediately compatible with any manifold implemented in geoopt, sidestepping the need for closed-form densities/normalizing constants that complicate VAE-style approaches on curved spaces.

The geometry-aware noise regularization is derived cleanly from a second-order Taylor/Bishop-style analysis and is shown (Appendix E, Figure S2) to meaningfully adapt to local curvature, giving an interpretable knob relating noise scale and manifold curvature.

The paper evaluates on three diverse, well-motivated real/synthetic datasets (cell-cycle scRNA-seq, synthetic hierarchical branching diffusion, human mitochondrial DNA haplogroups), which is a nice showcase of applicability across bioinformatics/geometric-structure problems.

Reproducibility effort is good: detailed appendices document training pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware, dataset construction, and additional ablations (noise vs. curvature sweeps, error bars), and code/data availability is mentioned.

The paper is honest about several limitations, e.g., explicitly noting that test-time comparisons are biased in favor of their model due to re-optimizing latents at test time, and discussing memory/scalability concerns of the encoder-free design.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim—that respecting the correct manifold geometry substantially improves the learned representation—is only weakly supported at test time. The authors themselves note test results are 'generally similar across methods' (Table 1) and that Euclidean spaces sometimes match or beat the specialized manifolds (e.g., Euclidean R^3 in Table 1, Euclidean R^2/Sphere with c=0.0 in Table 2 training rows), undermining the motivation for manifold-specific modeling.

The test-time evaluation protocol re-optimizes latents by maximizing log-likelihood while freezing the decoder, which the authors admit biases the comparison in favor of their own (encoder-free) model relative to encoder-based baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE); this makes the reported test superiority not a fair apples-to-apples comparison.

Because each latent is a free parameter (no encoder, no amortization), the strong training-set correlations/reconstruction numbers could partly reflect memorization/overfitting rather than genuinely better geometric structure, and this is not clearly disentangled from genuine generalization improvements in the test metrics.

Quantitative structure-preservation metrics are limited to Pearson/Spearman correlation between manifold and reference distances and simple reconstruction error (MAE/MSE/F1); no more rigorous manifold-embedding quality metrics (e.g., trustworthiness, continuity, tree-distortion measures) are used, and many differences between models fall within one standard deviation of each other, weakening claims of significance.

No baseline outside VAE-style manifold models is considered (e.g., classical hyperbolic embedding methods, other manifold-learning techniques for hierarchies), and no computational-cost/scalability comparison against baselines is provided despite scalability being flagged as a concern.

Some central results are qualitative/visual (UMAP vs. Poincaré plots) rather than quantitatively validated, and the paper acknowledges the current work lacks strict benchmarking with ground-truth-labeled synthetic data, leaving open how well the approach would generalize beyond the three case studies chosen.

strengths: The core idea—discarding the encoder and directly optimizing manifold-valued latents with a Riemannian optimizer while training only a decoder—is simple, elegant, and sidesteps the well-known difficulty of defining closed-form densities on general Riemannian manifolds (a real pain point for VAE-style approaches like S-VAE, P-VAE, hyperspherical/hyperbolic priors).

The geometry-aware noise regularization is a nice theoretical addition: it generalizes the classical Bishop (1995) noise-injection-as-Tikhonov-regularization result to the Riemannian setting via a second-order Taylor expansion, yielding an interpretable Tr(J^T Σ G^{-1} J) penalty that adapts to local curvature.

The method is architecture-agnostic and compatible with any manifold implemented in geoopt (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic/Lorentz, product manifolds, etc.), which is a practical advantage over bespoke VAE variants that each require manifold-specific densities and sampling schemes.

Three diverse case studies (synthetic branching diffusion with known tree structure, human mitochondrial DNA haplogroups, and single-cell cell-cycle transcriptomics) ground the method in real bioinformatics applications, and the qualitative visualizations (e.g., Poincaré embeddings recovering tree structure that UMAP/Euclidean fail to show) are compelling.

Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: detailed appendices on training protocols, hyperparameters, hardware, pseudocode for the training loop and noise injection, and dataset curation details are provided.

Honest discussion of limitations, including scalability concerns (decoder-only latents scale memory linearly with dataset size) and an explicit acknowledgment that test-time latent re-optimization biases comparisons in the method's favor.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly admits that its test-set evaluation protocol is biased in its own favor: latents are re-optimized at test time (via Schuster & Krogh's strategy) by directly maximizing likelihood with frozen decoder parameters, whereas baseline VAEs use amortized encoders. This undermines the fairness and interpretability of the main quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–3, which are the primary evidence for the paper's central claims.

Quantitative results are mixed and do not clearly support the claim that matching the data's intrinsic geometry improves performance: in Table 1, Euclidean R^3 achieves the best test MAE/MSE, and in Table 2 Euclidean/Spherical manifolds are competitive with or better than hyperbolic ones at low noise. The paper's own text concedes 'test results are generally similar across methods,' which weakens the significance of the contribution.

Technical novelty is modest: the approach largely combines two existing ingredients (the Deep Generative Decoder of Schuster & Krogh 2023, and off-the-shelf Riemannian optimization via geoopt) plus a regularizer that is a fairly direct curved-space extension of a well-known Euclidean result (Bishop 1995). There is limited new theory beyond a second-order Taylor approximation with no formal convergence or approximation-error guarantees.

The manifold (and its curvature) must be manually pre-specified per dataset rather than learned or selected automatically, which limits the practical 'unsupervised representation learning' framing and requires domain knowledge that may not be available in general settings.

Baselines used for comparison (S-VAE 2018, ΔVAE 2019, P-VAE 2019) are relatively dated; no comparison is made to more recent geometric/hyperbolic representation learning methods, making it hard to assess the state-of-the-art significance of the gains.

The empirical validation leans heavily on qualitative visual inspection (UMAP/Poincaré disk plots) for the central claims about capturing hierarchical/geometric structure, with limited rigorous quantitative ground-truth benchmarking; the authors themselves note this as needed future work ('more synthetic datasets with controllable ground truth geometries would help alleviate issues in cross-study comparisons').

Scalability is an acknowledged but unaddressed limitation: per-sample latent parameterization means memory grows linearly with dataset size, and no experiments probe behavior at larger scale (datasets used are modest, ~5-67k points).

strengths: The core idea is simple and elegant: replace encoder-based variational inference on manifolds (which requires closed-form densities, intractable normalizing constants, and Monte Carlo/series approximations for KL terms) with decoder-only maximum-likelihood estimation of per-sample latents via Riemannian optimization. This sidesteps a major source of complexity and brittleness in existing Riemannian VAE literature.

Because the method only needs a Riemannian optimizer (e.g., via geoopt) rather than a closed-form prior/posterior density, it is in principle compatible with a much larger class of manifolds than prior work, which is typically restricted to a few manifolds with known densities (sphere, Poincaré ball/Lorentz model).

The geometry-aware regularization derived from injecting noise through the exponential map and performing a second-order Taylor expansion is a nice theoretical contribution, generalizing the classical noise-as-Tikhonov-regularization result (Bishop, 1995) to curved spaces, and the appendix provides a clear closed-form analysis of how curvature and noise scale interact (Appendix E).

The paper validates the approach on three diverse and meaningfully different problems (synthetic hierarchical branching diffusion, human mitochondrial DNA haplogroup lineages, and single-cell cell-cycle transcriptomics), providing qualitative evidence (e.g., Poincaré embeddings recovering tree structure that UMAP/Euclidean embeddings fail to capture) that the learned geometry aligns with known structure.

Reasonable ablations are included (noise scale sweeps, curvature sweeps, comparison across three real baselines: S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE) along with extensive appendix material (pseudocode, manifold list, hardware details, additional figures) that aids reproducibility.

The limitations and future directions section is candid about scalability (decoder-only representations scale linearly with dataset size) and about the restricted scope of manifolds actually tested, which is good practice.
weaknesses: The quantitative improvements over Euclidean/baseline models are modest and often not favorable on held-out test data: in Table 1, Euclidean R^3 achieves the best test MAE/MSE, and differences in Pearson/Spearman correlations across manifolds mostly fall within one standard deviation of each other, undermining the central claim that matching the manifold to the data's intrinsic geometry yields a clearly superior learned representation in a generalizable sense.

The paper's own footnote (section 4.1) admits that "generalization performance is generally of little significance" for this dimensionality-reduction use case, yet test-set comparisons are still presented as evidence of comparative merit; moreover, Appendix C.1 states that test-time latents for the proposed method are found by directly maximizing likelihood (i.e., re-fitting per-sample codes), which it explicitly acknowledges "biases test reconstruction metrics in favor of our model" relative to amortized encoder-based baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE). This is a significant fairness/soundness concern for the comparative evaluation, since the proposed method and baselines are not evaluated under comparable test-time protocols.

No Euclidean decoder-only ablation (i.e., the original Deep Generative Decoder of Schuster & Krogh without manifold constraints) is included as a baseline, which would help isolate whether gains stem from the manifold prior itself versus simply from removing the encoder/amortization gap.

Although the appendix lists a wide range of manifolds available via geoopt (Stiefel, SPD, product manifolds, etc.), the empirical study only exercises a narrow set (Euclidean, sphere, torus, Lorentz/Poincaré), so the claimed generality to "any manifold" is not strongly demonstrated empirically.

The theoretical derivation of the geometry-aware regularizer relies on a first/second-order Taylor approximation of the exponential map and ignores higher-order terms without empirical validation of the approximation's accuracy or its breakdown point, beyond informally noting an "optimal noise regime" in Figure 3c.

Scalability is a real and only partially mitigated limitation: because representations are free per-sample parameters rather than amortized, memory grows linearly with the number of samples and there is no principled way to encode unseen data without re-optimizing, limiting applicability to very large datasets or streaming/inference settings.

Statistical rigor is limited to mean ± std over a small number of seeds (five for cell cycle/branching diffusion, three for hmtDNA) without formal significance testing, making it harder to assess whether reported differences between manifolds/methods are meaningful given overlapping error bars in several tables.

strengths: Simple, clean unifying idea: extend the encoder-free Deep Generative Decoder to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds by combining Riemannian (per-sample) latent optimization with standard neural decoders, avoiding intractable manifold densities/normalizing constants required by VAE-style approaches (vMF, wrapped normal, etc.).

The geometry-aware noise regularization is derived with a clear, principled second-order Taylor argument connecting Gaussian noise injection (scaled by the inverse metric) to an implicit Jacobian-based penalty tied to local curvature; this is a nice theoretical contribution distinguishing it from prior curvature-regularization work (Lee & Park, 2023) while avoiding expensive Hessian-vector computations.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across three qualitatively different domains (synthetic branching tree, cell-cycle scRNA-seq, human mtDNA haplogroups) with both qualitative visualizations and quantitative correlation/reconstruction/downstream-task metrics, plus sensible baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE).

Strong scalability/practicality story: Table 4 shows the method remains stable and fast as latent dimension grows to 500D, while VAE baselines and explicit curvature regularization break down or become infeasible — a meaningful practical advantage given real single-cell data has many genes/dimensions.

Reasonably thorough appendices covering training details, manifold list (via geoopt), ablations on noise scale vs. curvature, and additional downstream/generative-fidelity checks, supporting reproducibility; a reproducibility statement and code/data links are provided.
Honest treatment of limitations (memory growth with dataset size due to per-sample latents, lack of amortized inference, generative properties not the focus) rather than glossing over them.
weaknesses: Central quantitative results are mixed/marginal: in Table 1 (cell cycle) the proposed model's correlations and reconstruction errors are essentially statistically indistinguishable from S-VAE/ΔVAE baselines, undermining the claim of a clear empirical advantage in that case; the paper's main selling point ends up being scalability/stability rather than accuracy.

The novelty over Schuster & Krogh (2023)'s Deep Generative Decoder is somewhat incremental: the core contribution is essentially swapping Euclidean free-parameter latents for Riemannian-manifold latents via an off-the-shelf Riemannian optimizer (geoopt/RiemannianAdam), which, while useful, is a relatively small conceptual step; the paper could better delineate what specifically is technically novel versus straightforward composition of existing tools (geoopt, DGD, noise-as-regularization ideas from Bishop/An).

The evaluation lacks statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) despite reporting means ± std over only 3-5 seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., Table 1, Table 2) are meaningful versus noise, especially given overlapping error bars in several rows.

No direct comparison against amortized encoder-based general-geometry VAEs beyond the specific manifold cases studied (e.g., general Riemannian normal / wrapped-normal approaches like Kalatzis et al. 2020, Falorsi et al. 2018), despite the introduction motivating the work partly against 'general geometries' methods; only S-VAE (sphere), P-VAE/ΔVAE (hyperbolic) are compared, leaving the 'any manifold' unifying claim somewhat under-tested for genuinely heterogeneous/product manifolds beyond the toy torus case.

Test-time latent inference (freezing decoder, optimizing z via MAP) is compute-intensive per new sample and is not benchmarked for cost/quality versus a trained encoder at test time, which is an important practical trade-off for an 'encoder-less' method that is not fully explored quantitatively.

The claimed geometric interpretability/superiority of the learned manifold representations relies heavily on qualitative visual inspection (e.g., Figures 2-4) and correlation to somewhat noisy proxy ground truths (one-hot mutation distance, inferred cell-cycle phase from a separate model), which are imperfect ground truths and could bias conclusions in the paper's favor.

Ablation in Section 4.2/Figure 3c shows a clear tradeoff where increasing noise beyond ~0.9 degrades reconstruction (MSE rises sharply) even as correlation improves, and the paper does not provide a principled method for selecting sigma other than manual tuning per dataset, which weakens the 'plug-and-play' scalability narrative and could limit reproducibility across new datasets without careful hyperparameter search.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely useful problem: scaling Riemannian representation learning beyond a handful of simple manifolds (sphere, Poincaré ball) by removing the need for tractable amortized encoder densities, building cleanly on the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) idea and generalizing it to arbitrary manifolds via Riemannian optimization (RiemannianAdam/geoopt).

The geometry-aware noise regularization is derived with a clear second-order Taylor expansion connecting Gaussian noise injected via the exponential map to an implicit penalty on the Jacobian weighted by the inverse metric, giving a principled, computationally cheap (first-order) alternative to explicit curvature regularizers, which the paper shows break or become infeasible at higher latent dimension (Table 4).

Reasonably broad empirical coverage across three distinct real/synthetic datasets (cell-cycle scRNA-seq, synthetic branching diffusion trees, human mitochondrial haplogroup data) with several manifold choices (Euclidean, spherical, toroidal, hyperbolic/Lorentz) and baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE).

Strong reproducibility: code/data links, detailed appendices on training protocol, hardware, hyperparameters, and ablations (noise scale, curvature) are provided, and a clear limitations discussion (linear memory growth with dataset size, no amortized inference) is included honestly rather than hidden.

The scalability comparison (Table 4) showing baseline VAE variants with explicit curvature regularization numerically break or become infeasible at larger latent dimensions, while the proposed method scales smoothly, is a concrete and convincing practical advantage.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains over baselines are frequently marginal and within one standard deviation of each other (e.g., Table 1 cell-cycle correlations cluster tightly around 0.5–0.6 for essentially every manifold and baseline, with largely overlapping error bars), undermining the claim that geometry choice or the proposed method meaningfully improves alignment with the biological signal.

On the branching-diffusion benchmark (Table 2), the method 'significantly outperforms other models on the training data' but the authors themselves note 'the test results are generally similar across models,' and a footnote dismisses generalization as 'of little significance' for a dimensionality-reduction tool — this is a weak post-hoc justification for what looks like overfitting of the per-sample latent codes, a known risk of the encoder-less/MAP design.

The geometric regularization is not a free improvement but exposes an explicit reconstruction-vs-correlation trade-off (Figure 3c/S4: correlation increases but MSE monotonically worsens with noise level), and the right noise scale further interacts non-trivially with curvature (Appendix F), meaning practitioners must hand-tune two coupled hyperparameters per manifold/dataset without clear guidance on how to select them for new problems.

Removing the encoder eliminates amortized inference: representations for new/held-out data require solving a fresh per-sample MAP optimization at test time (as stated, following Schuster & Krogh 2023), which is a non-trivial scalability and usability cost that is not clearly discussed/quantified relative to standard encoder-based forward passes, partially undercutting the paper's 'highly scalable' framing.

The core technical contribution is incremental: it largely combines three existing ingredients (DGD's MAP/encoder-less framework, geoopt's Riemannian optimizers for arbitrary manifolds, and a Bishop/An-style noise-equals-regularization argument adapted to a non-Euclidean metric) rather than introducing fundamentally new theory or architecture; the main novel element is the small derivation in Section 3.1, which is reasonable but limited in depth.

Evaluation datasets, while real, are modest in scale and from a narrow domain (biological/genomic data); no comparison is made against more recent or more competitive general-manifold VAEs/approaches beyond the three selected baselines, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) is reported despite the close numerical margins across methods.

strengths: Proposes a simple, unifying encoder-free (MAP-based) framework for learning Riemannian latent representations on arbitrary manifolds, extending the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) idea to the Riemannian setting, which elegantly sidesteps the need for intractable manifold-specific densities and normalizing constants required by encoder-based VAE approaches (S-VAE, P-VAE, mixed-curvature VAE, etc.).

Introduces a principled, lightweight geometry-aware noise regularization derived via a second-order Taylor expansion, linking the injected noise covariance to the inverse Riemannian metric, and provides a clear theoretical derivation connecting it to Tikhonov-style regularization (Bishop 1995, An 1996).

Empirical validation spans three distinct and well-motivated case studies (synthetic branching diffusion tree, human mtDNA haplogroups, and cell-cycle scRNA-seq), covering different manifold types (spherical, hyperbolic, toroidal, product manifolds), which is a reasonably diverse testbed for a representation-learning method.

Demonstrates substantially better scalability/runtime stability versus VAE baselines and explicit curvature regularization, including cases where baselines break or become infeasible at higher latent dimension (Table 4), which is a meaningful practical advantage.

Thorough appendices with ablations (noise scale vs. curvature interaction, metric coherency over training, generative fidelity via discriminator test, downstream task utility) and a reproducibility statement with code/data links strengthen the empirical case.

The qualitative visualizations (e.g., Poincaré embeddings recovering tree/haplogroup structure that UMAP and Euclidean embeddings miss) provide intuitive, convincing support for the core claim that manifold choice matters and that the method respects prescribed geometry.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are mixed: on the branching diffusion task, test-set results are described as 'generally similar across methods' despite large training-set gains, and the Pearson/Spearman correlation improvements on cell cycle data are often within one standard deviation of baselines (Table 1), making the quantitative superiority of the method less clear-cut than the narrative suggests.

The decoder-only, per-sample latent parameterization fundamentally lacks amortized inference, meaning the method cannot encode new/held-out points without a separate post-hoc optimization procedure (as acknowledged, following Schuster & Krogh), and memory scales linearly with dataset size — a significant practical limitation for large-scale or streaming data scenarios that is only briefly discussed in the conclusion.

No standard deviations/uncertainty are reported for Table 3 (hmtDNA downstream utility) and several other key tables, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported differences between RGD and baselines.

The geometric regularization introduces a bias-variance-like tradeoff (Figure 3c) between local reconstruction accuracy and global geometric coherency that is not fully resolved — the paper shows correlation increases with noise up to a point then does not degrade much, but selection of optimal noise scale/curvature appears to require manual tuning per dataset, with no principled selection procedure provided (noted as future work).

Comparisons to baselines on identical latent dimensionality/architecture may still not be entirely fair, since baseline implementations were 'adjusted' to match the proposed architecture but hyperparameters were tuned separately; details of this tuning (e.g., search budget) are not reported, raising reproducibility concerns about whether baselines were given equal optimization effort.

The theoretical derivation of the geometric regularizer relies on first-order/second-order approximations (approximating the exponential map by identity, ignoring higher-order terms) whose accuracy for highly curved regions (e.g., near the boundary of the Poincaré ball) is not empirically validated beyond qualitative figures.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution is largely a straightforward generalization of DGD (Schuster & Krogh, 2023) to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds via existing tools (geoopt, RiemannianAdam), with the main new technical ingredient being the noise-based regularizer; this may limit the significance of the contribution relative to the engineering/combination effort.
